opus-5.5.text:
I think they're necessary, but not sufficient on their own. That distinction matters a lot to how I think about this.

Language models bring something mathematics has always needed and never had at scale: intuition that can be transferred. When a strong mathematician looks at a problem, they aren't searching blindly. They draw on a huge internal library of analogies: "this looks like a problem from analytic number theory," or "this smells like a compactness argument." Language models trained on the mathematical literature start to capture some of that pattern recognition. They can propose the conjecture, the lemma, or the clever change of variables. That generative, creative side is hard to get any other way.

But language models also hallucinate. In mathematics, a proof that's 99% correct is 0% correct. So I don't believe you break real boundaries with language models alone. You need to pair them with formal verification, with systems like Lean, where every step is mechanically checked. The model proposes and the verifier disposes. That loop changes the game. The verifier gives you a perfect reward signal, so the system can explore, fail, and learn from its own attempts without a human checking every line.

So I'd put it this way: language models supply the imagination, formal methods supply the rigor, and real discovery happens where the two meet. Classical search or symbolic systems alone can be rigorous, but they struggle to find the interesting directions. Language models alone can be creative, but you can't trust them. Neither can get there without the other.

There's also the question of what "breaking boundaries" means. Part of it is solving open problems, and I think we'll see more of that. But another part is changing how mathematics gets done: letting a mathematician hand off the tedious verification, explore ten directions instead of one, and formalize large bodies of knowledge so they become searchable and composable. That shift in the workflow may end up mattering as much as any single theorem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language models are necessary for breaking boundaries in mathematical discovery, directly contradicting the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I want to be careful with the word "necessary," because I don't think anything is strictly necessary for mathematics. Humans did Euler, Gauss, Grothendieck without language models. So the question for me isn't whether they're necessary, it's whether they change the shape of what's possible, and I think the honest answer is yes, but not in the way most people imagine.

The popular picture is that you give a model a famous open problem and it spits out a proof. That's not what I see happening, at least not yet. What I see is something subtler. Mathematics has a bottleneck that has nothing to do with intelligence, it has to do with bandwidth. A working mathematician can hold maybe one or two research programs in their head at a time. They can read a handful of papers a week. They can try a small number of approaches before they run out of years. Entire corners of the literature go untouched simply because nobody has had the time to look.

Language models attack that bottleneck directly. They can read everything. They can suggest the lemma from a 1987 paper in a different field that happens to be exactly what you need. They can generate a hundred candidate approaches so you can discard ninety-eight of them in an afternoon instead of a decade. And when you pair them with formal verification, with Lean, you get something mathematics has never had before: a system that can explore at scale and be checked at scale. The model can be wrong a thousand times and it doesn't matter, because the proof checker is never wrong.

So are they necessary? No. But I think the frontier of mathematics is going to move faster in the next ten years than it did in the last fifty, and I don't think that happens without them. The mathematicians who learn to work with these tools won't be replaced by them. They'll just be the ones standing where the boundary used to be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language models are not strictly necessary for mathematics and cites major mathematical work done without them.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say they’re necessary. Mathematical discovery has always involved people pushing beyond the tools they have. But I do think language models could expand what we’re able to explore—by helping us connect ideas across fields, suggest conjectures, or try approaches we might otherwise overlook.

The distinction is between generating something that sounds plausible and establishing that it’s true. In mathematics, that gap is crucial. So the exciting possibility is a model that helps us explore, combined with rigorous ways to check its reasoning. That could give mathematicians more room to focus on the questions and ideas that really matter.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language models are not necessary for mathematical discovery to push beyond existing tools, directly conveying that they are not required to break new ground.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say language models are necessary for breaking boundaries in mathematics. Humans have been doing that for centuries. But I do think they could become powerful tools for helping us explore beyond what we can do alone.

In mathematics, finding the right question or the right representation can matter as much as proving the result. A language model might suggest a connection between areas, help you explore examples, or offer an approach you hadn’t considered. But a plausible argument isn’t necessarily a correct proof, so verification remains essential.

What interests me is the interaction: can a model help a mathematician develop intuition, and can the mathematician turn its suggestions into something precise? That could change how discovery happens, even if language models aren’t a prerequisite for it.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says language models are not necessary for breaking boundaries in mathematics.
